name: Chautauqua chestnut oak
access: Free; Chautauqua Park is a public city park open daily.
transport: Boulder bus HOP/Chautauqua stop area; roughly 25 min walk from Pearl Street, or the seasonal Chautauqua shuttle.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 36 inches across at chest height, among the oaks of Chautauqua Park. It stands about 30 metres from the white oak on the same city tree tour.
story:
The City of Boulder says the largest chestnut oak in Colorado grows in Chautauqua Park, a long way from the eastern hardwood forests the species calls home. The city's notable tree tour gives its trunk as 36 inches across at chest height, about 91 centimetres, which works out to nearly three metres round.

There is a wrinkle in that crown. Colorado's state champion tree register lists two Boulder chestnut oaks a little thicker, at 37.5 and 38.1 inches, without saying exactly where they stand. Either the tour figure is older, or the register is measuring different trees. We give you the city's claim and the register's numbers side by side rather than pick one.

Chautauqua itself was founded in 1898 as a summer retreat for lectures and concerts, and is now on the National Register of Historic Places. The city says most of its trees were planted in 1903, when the grounds were laid out, and that a few are older. Which group this oak belongs to is not recorded, so we have not dated it. If you know, tell us.

It stands among the park's oaks, about 30 metres from a white oak the same tour singles out, so the two make one stop. The newest record of it we found is that 2021 city tour, so if you visit, a photograph would be welcome.

name: Chautauqua white oak
access: Free; Chautauqua Park is a public city park open daily.
transport: As bld_001; about 30 m from the chestnut oak.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in autumn, when it turns red to maroon. It stands in Chautauqua Park about 30 metres from the chestnut oak on the city's notable tree tour.
story:
Every autumn, reliably, this white oak turns red and then maroon. That is the City of Boulder's own description, in the notable tree tour its forestry team published in 2021, and it is the best reason to come here in October.

The tour also calls it the fourth largest white oak in Colorado. That ranking is harder to pin down. The state's champion tree register lists Boulder white oaks at 45.5, 43 and 36.5 inches across, in first, joint third and fifth place, and none of them sits cleanly at number four. Rankings shift as trees are measured again, so read fourth as the city's figure at the time of the tour.

White oaks belong to the forests of the eastern United States, and in Boulder they grow because people planted them. Chautauqua Park was founded in 1898, and the city says most of its trees went in when the grounds were laid out in 1903. This one's planting date is not recorded, so we have not given it an age.

It stands about 30 metres from a chestnut oak the city calls the largest in the state, which makes the pair an easy stop on a walk through the park. The newest record of it we found is the 2021 tour, so a recent photograph from a visitor would help.

best_time.label: October, when the city says it reliably turns red to maroon

name: Naropa sycamores

location.address: Naropa University, 2130 Arapahoe Ave, Boulder, CO

access: University campus grounds; the city includes it on its public tour, but no source states opening terms. Flagged: confirm grounds are open.
transport: Boulder bus along Arapahoe Ave; about 20 min walk from Pearl Street Mall.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the three large sycamores standing together beside the preserved 1903 Lincoln Elementary School building, on Naropa University's Arapahoe Avenue campus.
story:
Three of the largest sycamores in Colorado grow side by side on the grounds of a 1903 schoolhouse. The City of Boulder's notable tree tour says so, and adds that historic photographs show them planted not long after Lincoln Elementary School opened, which puts them at roughly 110 to 130 years old.

The school building still stands. It has been a Boulder landmark since 1989 and is now part of Naropa University's campus on Arapahoe Avenue, so the trees have shaded more than a century of students, first children and now adults.

Colorado's champion tree register lists three big Boulder sycamores, one 54 inches across and 95 feet tall, the others about 49 inches. They fit these three well, but the register does not say where its trees stand, so we cannot match the numbers to these trunks for certain.

We treat the three as one place to stand. You see them together, and they are the destination together.

One honest caveat. These are on a private university's grounds. The city includes them on its public tour, but we have not found Naropa's own terms for visitors, so look from the edge of the grounds if in doubt. The newest record of the trees is the 2021 city tour. If you go, tell us how they look.

name: Hale Science yellow buckeye

location.address: University of Colorado Boulder campus, near Hale Science Building, Boulder, CO

access: Free; CU Boulder campus grounds are open to walkers.
transport: Boulder bus to the University Memorial Center; the campus is a 15 min walk from Pearl Street.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big yellow buckeye among the old trees around Hale Science, the 1894 building on the CU Boulder campus.
story:
Hale Science went up on the University of Colorado campus in 1894, and the City of Boulder thinks most of the big trees around it followed in the early 1900s. One of them is this yellow buckeye, which the city's notable tree tour calls one of the largest of its kind in Colorado.

The age is the city's reasoning, not a planting record. Most likely, it says, planted in the early 1900s, so we give it as a little over a century and keep the range wide. The state's champion tree register lists a Boulder yellow buckeye at 32 inches across, in third place, though it does not say where that tree stands.

Yellow buckeye is a tree of the Appalachians and the Ohio Valley, and seeing one this big at the foot of the Rockies is the point of the visit.

The same city tour also featured a great cottonwood by Old Main, which was cut down in January 2022. That is a reminder that the tour is a few years old now. We found no newer record of the buckeye, so if you walk past Hale Science, a photograph or a word on how it is doing would help us.

name: Green Mountain Cemetery swamp white oak
access: Free; cemetery grounds open to visitors in daylight (not verified hours).
transport: No close stop confirmed; about 2.5 km from downtown Boulder, bike or car.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as Colorado's champion swamp white oak, 42 inches across in the state register. It stands in Green Mountain Cemetery in Boulder.
story:
The largest swamp white oak in Colorado grows in a Boulder cemetery. The City of Boulder's notable tree tour calls it a state champion, and the state's champion tree register agrees, listing Boulder's swamp white oak in first place at 42 inches across and 70 feet tall, about 107 centimetres and 21 metres.

Green Mountain Cemetery was established in 1905, and the city says most of its trees were planted around 1910. That is a statement about the cemetery, not a planting record for this oak, so its age, roughly 115 years, is a reasonable reading rather than a fact.

Swamp white oak is a tree of wet bottomlands in the eastern United States. Here it grows in a cemetery at the foot of the Rockies, and it has spent more than a century as a quiet witness to the city's funerals and Sunday visits.

The cemetery grounds are open to visitors, though we have not confirmed its hours. Please treat it as the burial ground it still is. The newest record of the tree we found is the city's 2021 tour, so if you visit, tell us how it looks.
